what: HA Sustainable Infrastructure (formerly Hannon Armstrong) invests in climate-related infrastructure: it provides equity and debt to solar, wind, battery storage, renewable natural gas and energy-efficiency projects, usually alongside the developers who build and run them.
customers: Clean-energy developers and utilities such as AES, Engie and others that want a capital partner for projects, and federal, state and municipal buildings for efficiency projects.
money: Its share of the earnings and cash of solar, wind, storage and other projects it co-owns.
Interest on loans to projects and fees for arranging and securitising financings.
moat: Long relationships with large developers and two decades of underwriting this asset class give HASI deal flow and data that generalist lenders lack. Its contracts sit behind long-term power purchase agreements, which makes the cash flows predictable.
risks: It borrows heavily: $3.8B of debt against $2.7B of equity. Its returns depend on the gap between what projects pay and what HASI pays to borrow.
US policy on clean-energy tax credits has turned less supportive, which could slow new projects.
Reported earnings jump around because of how it accounts for its project stakes, which makes the GAAP P/E of 34 hard to use.
The business grows by issuing shares and debt, so dilution is part of the model: diluted shares went from 88M in 2021 to 138M in 2025.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $213M in 2021 to $401M in 2025.
The forward P/E of about 15 on its adjusted earnings, plus a dividend yield of about 4.4%, is a reasonable price for a growing lender.
Data centres need large amounts of new power, and much of it will be solar and storage contracted with exactly the developers HASI funds.
Fourteen analysts average a $49 target, about 33% above the price.
watch: The spread between its portfolio yield and its cost of debt, and whether new investment volume holds up as tax credits change.
view: Ignore the trailing P/E of 34. HASI accounts for its project stakes with a method that books earnings when tax benefits are allocated rather than when cash arrives, so GAAP profit swings for reasons that say little about the business. The company’s own adjusted earnings, on which the forward P/E is about 15, are closer to what shareholders actually earn, and the 4.4% dividend is paid out of them.

Seen that way, HASI is a specialist lender and co-investor, and the question is the spread. It earns high single-digit yields on new projects and pays something like 6% on its debt; the difference, levered roughly 1.4 times, is the return. Rising rates squeezed that spread in 2023 and 2024, which is why the shares fell, and the share count rising from 88 to 138 million shows how growth has been funded.

What the market is pricing in is policy risk: if tax credits shrink, fewer projects get built and HASI’s pipeline thins. I think that is real but overdone, because the electricity demand from data centres has to be met with whatever can be built fastest, and that is still mostly solar and storage. At this price, with a 4% yield while you wait, I think the risk is paid for, but this is an income stock tied to interest rates, not a growth story.
bull: Power demand keeps projects coming, spreads widen as rates fall and the shares re-rate toward the analysts’ target.
bear: Tax-credit cuts dry up new projects and higher borrowing costs squeeze the spread that funds the dividend.
